task.scenario: Imagine that in the fictional country of “Polisia” protests broke out after disputed elections, the authorities tightened control over the media, and then announced a “state reform” and an intention to change the electoral system. Your task is not to describe the events one by one but to explain them as a single political process. Work out, Socratically, which elements of the course you need to apply to answer three questions: 1) what is the object and what is the subject of the political scientist’s analysis here; 2) which type of regime, party system and electoral system, and which source of legitimacy and mechanism of power are most likely; 3) which theories help explain why the conflict arose, how it may develop and what it will lead to in domestic and foreign policy. The result should be a coherent, concise political-science diagnosis and a well-founded forecast.
task.referenceSolution: The analysis has to connect the levels of the course step by step. First, establish that the object is the political sphere of Polisia as a whole, and the subject is the regularities of power, institutions, political behaviour, the regime and conflict. Then identify the regime by its features: if there is limited pluralism and control over elections and the media, but no total penetration into all spheres of life, it is authoritarianism; if there is a mass ideology, total propaganda, terror and an attempt to control private life, it is totalitarianism. Judged by its consequences for the party system, the electoral system is most likely either majoritarian, tending to reduce the number of parties, or mixed/proportional, if the authorities are trying to redistribute representation institutionally; the party system will depend on this design and on the depth of social cleavages. Legitimacy must be distinguished from legality: a government can be formally lawful yet lose society’s recognition, that is, become illegitimate; in that case it will rely above all on coercion, authority and manipulation rather than on voluntary recognition. The conflict should be treated as political because what is at stake is power and the rules for distributing it; it can be explained through theories of conflict, development crises and revolutions: a crisis of legitimacy and participation, relative deprivation, weak channels for expressing demands and the absence of “safety valves” raise the risk of escalation. If the protests are not channelled institutionally, the conflict may turn into a crisis and then into a revolutionary situation, or into authoritarian consolidation. For a broader forecast, political culture and socialisation (the level of trust in the authorities and readiness to participate) and elite theories (a split within the ruling class) are also useful, and for foreign policy, realism if the regime seeks support from force and balancing, or constructivism if it tries to redefine identity and the image of the enemy. Final diagnosis: Polisia is probably experiencing a deepening legitimacy crisis of an authoritarian regime; the authorities respond by tightening control and reforming institutions to preserve their dominance, and the outcome depends on whether the protests and elite splits can grow into a stable alternative or are suppressed through coercion and limited institutional adaptation.

key_points: The object and the subject of political science must be distinguished and this distinction applied to the case.
The likely type of political regime must be identified correctly by its features, not by the name in the constitution.
The regime must be linked to the type of electoral and party system, showing how they influence each other.
Legality must be distinguished from legitimacy, and the resources and mechanisms on which power rests must be named.
The conflict must be explained as a struggle for power and the rules of the game, not simply as “unrest”.
At least two or three theoretical frameworks from the course must be used: conflict/crisis/revolution, political culture and socialisation, elites, regimes, institutions.
The logic of escalation must be shown: from latent conflict to crisis and possible outcomes.
Internal dynamics must be linked to possible foreign-policy consequences, mentioning one of the IR paradigms where relevant.
The answer must be a coherent political-science diagnosis and forecast, not a list of terms.
rubricSpec.answer_reached_criteria: The student has reached the answer if they explain the case consistently and without internal contradictions through the level of object/subject, the type of regime, institutions, legitimacy, conflict and a forecast, tying these into a single well-argued scheme.

turns.content: Let me separate the levels first. The object of analysis is the political sphere of Polisia as a whole, and the subject is the regularities of power, institutions, political behaviour and conflict that show up here.
Good, you have separated the object and the subject. By which features in the task would you identify the type of regime?

Elections are held, although disputed, and there are protests, so pluralism is limited but not destroyed. The authorities control the media, but nothing is said about a mass ideology, terror or control over private life. So this is authoritarianism, not totalitarianism.
How does the announced reform of the electoral system fit into this picture?

Most likely the authorities want to strengthen the majoritarian element: under Duverger’s law a majoritarian system reduces the number of parties, and the party system will shift towards a dominant-party system of the ruling party. So they change the electoral rules to lock in their advantage institutionally.
What does the government rely on, then, if the election results are disputed?

Formally the government is legal, since the elections took place according to the law, but its legitimacy, that is, society’s recognition, is falling. Since there is little voluntary recognition, the government relies on coercion and manipulation, and control over the media is exactly a tool of manipulation.
How would you explain why the conflict arose and how it might develop?

Conclusion. The object is the political sphere of Polisia, the subject is the regularities of power and conflict. The regime is authoritarian: limited pluralism, control over the media and elections, but no total control. The electoral reform is an attempt to lock in the dominance of the ruling party through majoritarian rules. The government is legal but is losing legitimacy, so it rests on coercion and manipulation. The conflict is political because the dispute is about power and the rules for distributing it; it is explained by a crisis of legitimacy and participation and by relative deprivation, while there are no legal channels for expressing demands. Forecast: if the protests are not channelled through institutions, the conflict will turn into a crisis and possibly a revolutionary situation, especially if the elites split; otherwise the government will consolidate authoritarianism through coercion and limited reforms. In foreign policy, following the logic of realism, the regime will look for powerful allies and try to balance.

turns.content: Here is my diagnosis. The object of analysis is the political sphere of Polisia, the subject is the regularities of power, institutions, political behaviour and conflict. By its features the regime is authoritarian: there are elections, but they are disputed, pluralism is limited and the media are controlled, while there is no mass ideology, terror or control over private life, so it is not totalitarianism. The electoral reform is probably a move to majoritarian rules: according to Duverger they reduce the number of parties and lead to a dominant-party system of the ruling party, although with deep social cleavages the opposition may consolidate. The government keeps its legality but is losing legitimacy, society’s voluntary recognition, so it relies on coercion, manipulation and what is left of its authority. The conflict is political: it is about power and the rules for distributing it. It can be explained by the theory of development crises (a crisis of legitimacy and participation) and the theory of relative deprivation: people’s expectations exceed what the system gives them, and there are no “safety valves”. The logic of development: after the disputed elections a latent conflict became open; if demands are not channelled through institutions, it will grow into a political crisis and possibly a revolutionary situation, especially if the elites split and trust is low in the political culture; if the elites stay united, authoritarian consolidation with limited institutional adaptation is likely. In foreign policy, according to realism the regime will seek support from force and balance, and according to constructivism it will construct the image of an external enemy. In sum: Polisia faces a growing legitimacy crisis of an authoritarian regime that holds on to power by control and by rebuilding institutions, and the outcome depends on whether protest and an elite split can form a stable alternative.
It seems to me this is just unrest after the elections.
What distinguishes unrest from a political conflict if you look at what the sides are arguing about?

Let me correct myself: the dispute is about who gets power and under which rules, so this is a political conflict, not unrest. For a political scientist the object here is the whole political life of Polisia, and the subject is the regularities of the struggle for power and of how institutions work.
What do the features in the task say about the nature of the regime?

There are elections and an opposition, but the elections are disputed and the media are controlled, so this is not a democracy. It is not totalitarianism either: there is no single ideology and no terror. I would call it competitive, hybrid authoritarianism: formal democratic institutions remain, but the government bends the rules to suit itself.
What could a change of the electoral system mean for parties and representation?

If the government introduces a mixed system with a high threshold or draws districts in its own favour, small parties will not get in and the opposition will fragment; the party system will become a dominant-party system. Although if society is deeply divided, the opposition may unite.
What happens to the recognition of the government meanwhile, and what does it rest on?
The government remains legal, but its legitimacy is falling: people do not accept the election results. So it relies on coercion, control of information and manipulation rather than on consent.
How would you tie all of this into a final diagnosis and forecast?

Everything forms one chain: the disputed elections undermined legitimacy, the government responded with coercion and media control, and with the “state reform” it is trying to rebuild institutions, the electoral and party system, around its own dominance. This is a conflict over power and the rules of the game; in terms of the theory of development crises it is a crisis of legitimacy and participation, and in terms of relative deprivation theory it is a gap between people’s expectations and what the system gives them. Forecast: if demands find no institutional channels and the elites split, the conflict will turn into a political crisis and possibly a revolutionary situation; if the elites stay united, the regime will consolidate through repression and limited concessions. Externally, following the logic of realism, the regime will seek the support of strong allies, and following constructivism it will create the image of an external enemy.

turns.content: The object is the political sphere of Polisia, and the subject is the regularities of power, institutions and conflict in it.
Which features in the task help to identify the type of regime?

There are elections, but they are disputed, the media are controlled, and at the same time there is no mass ideology and no terror. So the regime is authoritarian, neither totalitarian nor democratic.
How does the electoral reform relate to this?

The government changes the electoral rules to keep its dominance: according to Duverger a majoritarian system reduces the number of parties, and the party system moves towards a dominant-party system.
What does the government rest on in this situation?

It is legal but is losing legitimacy, because part of society does not recognise the elections. So its support shifts towards coercion and control over information. The conflict here is political: it is a struggle for power and the rules for distributing it.
What conclusion and forecast follow from all this?

Conclusion: in Polisia an authoritarian regime is going through a legitimacy crisis after disputed elections and responds to protest with media control and by rewriting the electoral rules to lock in its power. Forecast: if the protesters have no legal channels of influence, the conflict will grow from protests into a political crisis; if the government keeps its coercive resources, authoritarian consolidation with cosmetic reforms is more likely.

At the same time the government is legal but is losing legitimacy, so it relies on coercion and manipulation. If the elections were disputed, the government is formally lawful, it has legality. But if people don’t recognise it, its legitimacy falls. These are different things.
Since there is little voluntary recognition, the government rests on coercion, meaning media control and the security forces, and on manipulation, partly on what is left of its authority.
The conflict is political because the dispute is not about everyday matters but about power and the rules for distributing it, that is, about elections.

Why it arose: a crisis of legitimacy and participation, people have no channels to express their demands, and elections don’t work as a safety valve. Plus relative deprivation: expectations are higher than what people get.

Development: if the protests are not channelled through institutions, the conflict will go from latent to open, then a crisis, and it may reach a revolutionary situation. Or the government will suppress the protest and consolidate authoritarianism.

Another important thing is whether the elites split: if part of the ruling class goes over to the protesters, the regime may fall. And political culture: if trust in the government is low and readiness to participate is high, the protests will grow.
Foreign policy: according to realism the regime will look for strong allies and balance, and according to constructivism it may construct the image of an external enemy to rally society.

Conclusion: the object is the political sphere of Polisia, the subject is the regularities of power and conflict. The regime is authoritarian: limited pluralism, control over the media and elections, no total control. The electoral reform is an attempt to institutionally lock in the dominance of the ruling party, and the party system is moving towards a dominant-party system. The government is legal but is losing legitimacy, so it rests on coercion and manipulation. The conflict is political, about power and the rules of the game; it is explained by a crisis of legitimacy and participation and by relative deprivation. Forecast: either escalation to a crisis and a revolutionary situation if the elites split, or authoritarian consolidation through coercion and limited reforms; in foreign policy, realist balancing or constructing an enemy image.
